chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi and Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him: Is the testimony of the people of one (religious) community valid from other than the people of their own community? He said: Yes, when they cannot be found from the people of their own community, the testimony of others is valid. It is indeed not right for anyone's right to be lost.

key_terms.حَقّ: Right, entitlement; an inviolable claim that must be protected.
key_terms.شَهَادَة: Testimony; the act of giving legal witness. A cornerstone of Islamic jurisprudence.
key_terms.مِلَّة: Religious community or nation; refers to a body of people defined by their faith.

ai.seo_question: Is testimony from non-Muslims valid in Islamic law when Muslim witnesses are unavailable?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) rules that testimony from members of a different religious community (e.g., non-Muslims testifying in a Muslim's case) is admissible when witnesses from the same community cannot be found. The overriding principle is that no one's legal right should be wasted or forfeited due to the unavailability of same-faith witnesses. This ruling is particularly relevant to the context of wills and bequests made during travel, where the available witnesses may be from a different faith.
